Field surveys of the screaming hairy armadillo (Chaetophractus vellerosus) in the semiarid regions of central Argentina provide critical baseline data on its life history. Neonates emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 37.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 37.8 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the altricial state of newborn offspring in this genus. This birth weight was estimated based on scaling relationships observed in the congeneric species Chaetophractus villosus, where neonatal mass averages 113.4 grams in adults weighing approximately 3000 grams. The gestation period, during which the embryo undergoes organogenesis and foetal development within the uterine environment, lasts for 68 days [tg = 68 days] when females are maintained at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that falls within the 60- to 75-day range reported for other armadillos. This relatively brief gestation, coupled with the small size of the altricial neonate, suggests a reproductive strategy that prioritizes rapid offspring production over extended intrauterine provisioning. The foetal membrane stage and subsequent parturition appear to be timed to coincide with seasonal resource pulses in the species' xeric habitat, though direct observational data remain limited.

As the altricial neonate develops into a suckling juvenile, the timing of nutritional milestones provides insight into maternal investment strategies. The onset of weaning, marking the transition from exclusive milk ingestion to solid food consumption, is recorded at 55 days since birth [tx = 55 days since birth] under the same thermal regime of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This dietary transition represents a critical period of nutritional emancipation, during which the lactation-dependent offspring must begin processing exogenous food items. The pre-weaning juvenile remains dependent on the lactating female's milk for over seven weeks, a duration that aligns with the slow life-history pace typically observed in xenarthrans. Following weaning, the juvenile enters a period of rapid somatic growth, during which its body mass increases substantially as it learns to forage for invertebrates and plant matter independently. Field researchers have noted that although the weaned juvenile is nutritionally independent, it may continue to associate with the mother for several additional weeks, likely gaining experience in predator avoidance and resource location before fully dispersing from the natal territory.

Reproductive output in Chaetophractus vellerosus is constrained by a modest annual allocation strategy. Females typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with each litter consisting of two pups [N_R_i = each litter consisting of two pups]. These two components yield a total annual reproductive output of two pups per year, a relatively low fecundity that is characteristic of armadillos and other long-lived mammals with extended parental care periods. The maximum reproductive rate was documented in individuals maintained at a constant body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], reflecting the thermal conditions under which peak physiological performance occurs. This single-annual-litter strategy likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a diet of patchily distributed invertebrates and the substantial metabolic costs of lactation in a moderately sized mammal. The screaming hairy armadillo's slow reproductive tempo contrasts sharply with that of many rodents of similar body mass, which may produce several litters within a single breeding season. The reliance on a single, well-timed reproductive event per year suggests that females must carefully synchronize ovulation and subsequent parturition with periods of peak food abundance in the austral spring and summer months.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species. Females attain a maximum adult body mass, or asymptotic weight, of approximately 1100 grams [Wwi = approximately 1100 grams], with field records ranging from 257 grams to 1126 grams depending on local habitat quality and seasonal fluctuations in resource availability. Males, by contrast, reach a larger ultimate wet weight of approximately 1200 grams [Wwi = approximately 1200 grams], with a documented range spanning from 543 grams to 1329 grams. This size advantage in males is consistent with observations in other dasypodid armadillos and is likely linked to intrasexual competition for access to receptive females during the breeding season. The substantial intraspecific variation in adult body mass reflects the species' ability to modulate growth trajectories in response to environmental conditions, particularly during the juvenile and sub-adult phases. Researchers have noted that individuals inhabiting more productive alluvial soils tend to achieve higher asymptotic masses than those occupying degraded or overgrazed areas, indicating that food availability is a primary determinant of ultimate body size. This plasticity in adult body mass may buffer populations against interannual variation in precipitation and prey abundance.

Under the thermal conditions typical of resting metabolic studies in this species (35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]), the maximum longevity was estimated from captive individuals at approximately 16.2 years [am = approximately 16.2 years], the basal metabolic rate averaged 306.40 milliliters per hour [JOi = 306.40 milliliters per hour], and puberty was reached at 274.5 days since birth [tp = 274.5 days since birth]. This relatively extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly 5913 days when calculated on a daily basis, places the species among the longest-lived xenarthrans relative to its body size. The metabolic rate is notably low compared to eutherian mammals of equivalent mass, a pattern consistent with the reduced metabolic intensity observed across the armadillo lineage. The physiological trade-off between a low resting metabolic rate and an extended lifespan is a recurring theme in comparative analyses of mammalian aging, and the screaming hairy armadillo exemplifies this relationship. The timing of sexual maturation allows young females to participate in their first breeding season during the austral spring following their birth year, thereby maximizing the likelihood of successful reproduction before the onset of winter resource scarcity.
